q: One beer on the sheet is marked 12 and another 70 on the same scale, and the second will taste far more bracing. What is being measured?
exp: International Bitterness Units count isomerised hop acids dissolved in the finished beer. A mass-market lager sits in the high single figures, a pilsner in the thirties or forties, and a modern double IPA can run past eighty.

q: The density of the liquid is read before the yeast goes in and again once fermentation has finished, and the gap tells the brewer how much sugar was consumed. What is the first reading called?
exp: Water is the reference point at 1.000, so a wort at 1.050 carries a substantial load of dissolved sugar. The difference between the two readings converts directly into alcohol, and the proportion consumed is the attenuation.

q: A guest wants two or three glasses across a long evening without losing the thread of the conversation. Which figure on your list should guide the recommendation?
exp: Beer covers an enormous range, from a three percent mild to a fourteen percent barleywine, so strength is the number that governs the pace of an evening. A serving size that is sensible for one of those is reckless for the other.

q: One beer measures sixty-five bitterness units and tastes balanced, while another measures forty and tastes searing. What explains the reversal?
opts: The figure counts hop aroma rather than bitter compounds
The figure is taken on the wort rather than on the finished beer
Residual sweetness and body mask perceived bitterness
The scale runs backwards, so the lower figure means the more bitter beer
exp: Perceived bitterness is a ratio against malt sweetness, so the figure alone does not predict how a beer tastes and brewers talk about balance rather than raw units. A big sweet double IPA carries bitterness that would be punishing in a thin, dry beer.

q: Neglected draught lines grow a film of yeast, bacteria and beer stone that turns everything poured through them cloudy and sour. How often should a working system be cleaned?
exp: A fortnight is the usual industry benchmark, and busy lines carrying unfiltered or heavily hopped beer need attention sooner. No amount of care in the cellar rescues beer that has been dragged through a dirty line.

q: A long run from a cold room to a bar tower at the far end of the building needs more push than carbon dioxide alone can supply without over-carbonating the beer. What is blended in?
exp: Nitrogen dissolves poorly, so it supplies pressure without inflating the carbonation of the beer behind it. Air would oxidise the beer and introduce bacteria, which is why it was abandoned as a dispense gas.

q: A tulip, a tall weizen glass and a broad goblet all sit behind the same bar. What is the glass mainly doing for the beer?
opts: Altering the bitterness of the beer
Shaping the head and steering the aroma to the nose
Changing the carbonation level of the beer
Slowing oxidation over the course of an hour
exp: A collar of foam holds volatile aroma above the liquid, and the width of the rim decides how much of it reaches the drinker. Shape also governs how fast the beer warms in the hand, which matters for the stronger styles.

q: Poured straight from the fridge at three degrees, a Belgian tripel and an imperial stout both taste of almost nothing. What does serving them warmer restore?
opts: Aroma and complexity, which cold suppresses
exp: Volatile compounds need warmth to leave the liquid, so a very cold strong beer is mute. Crisp lagers are served cold for the opposite reason, since coldness is much of their appeal and there is less aroma to lose.

q: The glass is held at forty-five degrees for most of the pour and straightened at the end. What is the pourer actually controlling?
opts: The rate at which the keg empties
exp: Beer knocked straight into an upright glass releases its gas as foam and leaves the liquid beneath flat. A head of the right depth is part of the style, so pouring to avoid foam altogether is as much a mistake as drowning the glass in it.

q: Charred, grilled and heavily roasted flavours on the plate find a direct echo in one class of beer rather than a contrast. Which?
exp: The crust on the meat and the roast in the malt come from the same browning reactions, so the flavours run in parallel rather than against each other. The same resemblance carries the pairing on to chocolate and coffee puddings.

q: Briny raw shellfish is served in Dublin and Galway beside a dark beer that is low in alcohol, dry and roasty. Which beer is it?
exp: Roast bitterness plays against the salt while the creamy texture flatters the shellfish, and the modest strength keeps the beer from swamping it. It is among the oldest surviving beer pairings in the trade.

q: A hop-forward beer poured beside a sweet dessert turns harsh and metallic in the glass. What has happened?
opts: The cold of the dessert has muted the malt
The sugar has raised the actual alcohol content of the beer
The dessert has stripped the carbonation out of the beer
Sugar in the dish has sharpened perceived bitterness
exp: Sweetness in the food pushes up the perceived bitterness and acidity of whatever is drunk alongside it, exactly as it does with a dry wine. A pudding wants a beer at least as sweet as itself, which is why a doppelbock or a fruit lambic answers better.

q: The Garonne and the Dordogne converge to form which estuary?
exp: The two rivers meet north of the city to form the Gironde estuary. Left Bank and Right Bank are defined by which side of that water a vineyard sits on.

q: A merchant offers you a Left Bank red. Which grape most likely leads its blend?
exp: Left Bank gravel suits Cabernet Sauvignon, which usually dominates there. The Right Bank's cooler clay and limestone favour Merlot instead.

q: Entre-Deux-Mers sits between which two rivers?
exp: The name means between two seas, though the two waters are tidal rivers. The appellation itself is used for dry white wine only.

q: Of these appellations, which one lies on the Right Bank?
exp: Pomerol and Saint-Emilion are Right Bank. Margaux, Saint-Julien and Pessac-Leognan all sit on the Left Bank.
